content: Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF) is a disease transmitted by ticks and is prevalent in parts of Asia, Europe, and Africa. Since the year 2000, outbreaks of this infection have been reported in countries such as Turkey, Iran, Russia, Uganda, and Pakistan. High-quality general supportive medical care has been shown to reduce mortality in affected individuals. However, there is ongoing uncertainty and debate regarding the use of the antiviral drug ribavirin for treating CCHF. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of ribavirin in treating individuals with CCHF. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and CINAHL. Additionally, clinical trial registries such as the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched for ongoing studies. The search was completed on October 16, 2017. Experts in the field were also contacted to identify further studies. The inclusion criteria for the analysis encompassed randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized studies (NRSs) with more than 10 participants designed as cohort studies with comparators, and case-control studies. Two reviewers independently assessed the eligibility of studies, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data. For non-randomized studies, the ROBINS-I tool was used to assess the risk of bias. The main analysis included studies with low, moderate, or high risk of bias, while a separate analysis was conducted for studies with a critical risk of bias. Five studies met the inclusion criteria for the main analysis: one RCT with 136 participants and four non-randomized studies with 612 participants. Eighteen non-randomized studies with a critical risk of bias were excluded, as none of these studies adequately controlled for confounding factors. The evidence regarding the effectiveness of ribavirin in reducing mortality is highly uncertain. The RCT reported a risk ratio (RR) of 1.13 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.29 to 4.32) with very low-certainty evidence. Similarly, three non-randomized studies reported an RR of 0.72 (95% CI 0.41 to 1.28) with very low-certainty evidence. The impact of ribavirin on the length of hospital stay is also unclear. The RCT reported a mean difference (MD) of 0.70 days (95% CI -0.39 to 1.79), while one non-randomized study reported an MD of -0.80 days (95% CI -2.70 to 1.10), both with very low-certainty evidence. The evidence is also insufficient to determine whether ribavirin reduces the need for platelet transfusions. The RCT reported an RR of 1.23 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.96) with very low-certainty evidence. Regarding adverse effects, including haemolytic anaemia and treatment discontinuation, there is insufficient data to determine whether ribavirin increases the risk of these events in individuals with CCHF. One non-randomized study examined the effect of administering ribavirin and supportive care within four days of symptom onset compared to after four days. Mortality was lower in the group receiving early supportive care and ribavirin. However, it is not possible to distinguish whether the observed benefit was due to ribavirin, early supportive care, or a combination of both. In a subsidiary analysis, 18 studies compared individuals receiving ribavirin with those who did not. All of these studies had a critical risk of bias due to confounding factors, which likely influenced the mortality estimates favoring ribavirin. In conclusion, the effectiveness of ribavirin for treating Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever remains uncertain. Non-randomized studies are frequently cited as evidence of ribavirin's efficacy, but these studies are subject to a high risk of bias.
